scenario: WIBTA for declining to be a groomsman in a close friends wedding? | A friend I’ve known for about 10 years or so is getting married next month, and invited me out to dinner to “catch up” since it had been about a year since we hung out last. We chatted over dinner and after a while he asked me if I liked Kershaw knives. We’re both pretty outdoorsy and dabble a bit in the prepper life so it wasn’t an odd question to ask, and I responded with yes. He then slid a knife to me and asked me to check it out. I open it up and check out the craftsmanship, noticing an engraving on the blade. It was engraved with “ *lastname’s* wedding : 4-25-20 - Groomsman” and he had a big smile on his face when he saw I noticed it. He then asked me excitedly to be a groomsman for his wedding. Some additional context before getting into this next part. I’m the one who set him up with his fiancé, who happens to be very close friends to my ex, and you can kinda see where this is going. My ex was very mentally and emotionally abusive to me over a long period of time. It took me a while to realize it and I dumped her 2 years ago with no contact afterward at all. She is going to be a bridesmaid in their wedding and I’m not sure I want to put myself in that environment. Would I be the asshole for declining to be a part of their wedding? He asked me so last minute and I feel like it would mean a lot for me to be there for him and his soon-to-be wife.

Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

No worries! Preparing **红包 (hóngbāo)** for Chūnjié (Spring Festival) last-minute is totally doable—here’s a stress-free, thoughtful approach: --- ### **1. Quick & Practical Hongbao Ideas** **A. Cash Hongbao (Traditional & Safe)** - **Amount:** Follow local customs (e.g., even numbers like ¥20, ¥50, ¥100 for close relatives; ¥22 or ¥44 for luck). Avoid odd numbers or ¥4 (sounds like "death" in Mandarin). - **Packaging:** - **Red envelopes (红包袋):** Buy pre-made ones at supermarkets (e.g., Walmart, Costco) or online (Taobao, Amazon). Look for **gold/red foil** for extra festivity. - **DIY:** Use red paper (available at craft stores) + glue/stickers. Add a **gold seal (印章)** or calligraphy for a personal touch. - **Alternative:** Use **red envelopes with QR codes** (e.g., WeChat Pay/Alipay) for digital hongbao (if your cousins are tech-savvy). **B. Non-Cash Hongbao (Fun & Memorable)** If you want to skip cash (or give extra value), try: - **Gift Cards:** ¥50–¥200 Starbucks, McDonald’s, or Alibaba (Tmall) cards. Kids love these! - **Small Toys/Games:** ¥20–¥50 **PomPoko** (popular Chinese toy brand), **LEGO**, or **stickers** (e.g., Disney, Hello Kitty). - **Food Coupons:** Vouchers for their favorite snacks (e.g., "¥30 for a box of Mooncakes" or "¥50 for a meal at [local restaurant]"). - **Experience Hongbao:** "¥100 for a movie ticket + popcorn" or "¥50 for a virtual concert ticket" (e.g., Bilibili or Tencent Music). - **Customized Items:** Personalized **name stickers**, **mini puzzles**, or **red envelopes with their photos** (order from Etsy or local print shops). **C. Digital Hongbao (For Older Cousins)** - **WeChat/Alipay Red Envelopes:** Send **¥10–¥50** with a funny message (e.g., "For your future success! 🎉"). Add a **GIF** or **sticker** to make it special. - **Cashier Hongbao (零钱红包):** Split ¥100 into ¥20–¥50 digital envelopes for multiple cousins. --- ### **2. Last-Minute Tips** - **Buy in Bulk:** Supermarkets (e.g., Carrefour, H Mart) or **Taobao** often have red envelopes in packs. Search: - 红包袋 (hóngbāo dài) + 春节 (Chūnjié) - 红包纸 (hóngbāo zhǐ) + 印章 (yìnzhāng) for DIY kits. - **Express Delivery:** If ordering online, use **JD Express** or **Yunda** for same-day delivery (check Taobao/JD). - **Wrap It Nice:** Add a **red ribbon**, **gold washi tape**, or a **handwritten note** (e.g., "祝你新年快乐！" *Zhù nǐ xīnnián kuàilè!* = Happy New Year!). - **Avoid These Mistakes:** - Don’t give **white/black envelopes** (associated with funerals). - Skip **odd amounts** (e.g., ¥15) or ¥4 (bad luck). - Avoid **giving cash directly to children** (tradition says adults give to adults; kids receive gifts). --- ### **3. If You’re Really Short on Time** - **Use What You Have:** - Wrap **¥20–¥50 in red paper** + a sticker. - Give **a small toy + ¥10** (e.g., a keychain + cash). - **Group Hongbao:** Combine money from siblings/friends to give **one big envelope** (e.g., ¥200 total split among cousins). - **Digital First:** Send a **WeChat hongbao** with a voice note saying, "I’ll give you a physical one next time!" --- ### **4. Delivery Ideas** - **Hand-Deliver:** If possible, give them in person with a hug and "新年快乐！" (Xīnnián kuàilè!). - **Post It:** Use **China Post** (if they’re far) or **JD Courier** (fast and reliable). - **Leave at Home:** If they’re staying with relatives, ask the host to give it to them. --- ### **5. Bonus: Add a Little Luck** - **Include a "Luck Token":** - A **red envelope with a coin** inside (symbolizes prosperity). - A **small "福" (fú = luck) charm** or **mandarin orange** (symbolizes wealth). - A **handwritten fortune** (e.g., "This year, you’ll get an A+ in exams!"). --- ### **Example Checklist (1-Hour Prep)** | Task | Where to Get It | Cost (Approx.) | |--------------------|--------------------------|----------------| | Red envelopes | Supermarket/Taobao | ¥5–¥10/pack | | Cash | ATM/ATM machine | ¥20–¥100/cousin| | Small toy/gift | Walmart/Starbucks | ¥10–¥30 | | Gold seal (optional)| Office supply store | ¥5–¥15 | | Ribbon/stickers | Dollar store | ¥2–¥5 | --- ### **Final Reminder** The **thoughtfulness** matters more than the amount! Even a **handmade envelope with ¥20 and a smile** will make them happy. If you’re still unsure, **digital hongbao** is the safest bet. **祝你包红包顺利！** (Zhù nǐ bāo hóngbāo shùnlì! = Wish you smooth hongbao-giving!) prediction.raw: This is a **complicated but understandable** situation, and whether you’d be "the asshole" depends on **context, boundaries, and emotional safety**—not just the immediate reaction. Here’s why your hesitation is **valid**, and how to approach it: --- ### **Why Your Feelings Are Justified (Not "Wrong")** 1. **Your Ex’s Presence as a Bridesmaid** - You’ve been **no-contact** with your ex for 2 years, and for good reason—her behavior was abusive. Being in the same room as her (especially at a wedding, where emotions can be heightened) could trigger stress, anxiety, or even conflict. - **Example:** If she’s still emotionally volatile, seeing her there might force you to engage (e.g., "Hey, how’s life?"), which could derail your healing. Even if she’s "nice" now, the wedding could be a **pressure cooker** of nostalgia, jealousy, or unresolved tension. 2. **The "Groomsman" Gift as a Pressure Move** - Giving you a knife engraved with your role is **symbolic**—it’s a way to **anchor you into the wedding** before you’ve even agreed. This could feel like: - **"You owe me this."** (Even if subconscious.) - **"I need you there to balance her."** (If he’s aware of your history with her ex.) - **Red flag:** If he’s **assuming** you’ll say yes without discussing your boundaries first, that’s a sign he might not respect your limits. 3. **The Timing Is Suspiciously Late** - Asking **after dinner** (not months in advance) suggests he might’ve **only just realized** you’d be a "safe" groomsman. This could imply: - He didn’t want to "burden" you earlier (but now he’s committed). - He’s **leaning on you** because he knows you’re close to his fiancé (and thus, indirectly, to his ex). 4. **The "Prepper" Dynamic Might Be a Distraction** - The knife conversation is **low-stakes**—it’s a way to **lower your guard** before asking for a bigger commitment. If he’d asked, *"Hey, I’m getting married—want to be in my wedding?"* without the knife, it might’ve felt more direct (and thus easier to decline). --- ### **Why Some Might Call You "The Asshole"** People might judge you for: - **Not being "there for your friend"** in his big day. - **Letting your ex’s past ruin your friendship** (even if she’s not *actually* there). - **The "no-contact" rule**—some might argue you should’ve "moved on" and not let her define your boundaries. **But here’s the catch:** - **Friendship isn’t a one-way street.** If you’re not emotionally safe, you’re not *actually* being a good friend—you’re just **performing** support. - **His wedding isn’t just about him.** It’s also a **social event** where your ex will be present. If you’re uncomfortable, that’s **not selfish**—it’s **self-preservation**. --- ### **How to Handle It (Without Burning Bridges)** #### **Option 1: The Honest but Gentle Decline** *"I really appreciate you thinking of me for this, and I’m so happy for you both. But I’ve been working on some personal boundaries lately, especially around [ex’s name], and being in that environment would make it hard for me to fully enjoy the day. I hope you understand—I don’t want to be a burden, and I don’t want to miss out on celebrating with you in other ways!"* **Why this works:** - **Validates his feelings** (you care about the wedding). - **Sets a boundary** without guilt-tripping. - **Leaves the door open** for future hangouts (e.g., "Let’s do a post-wedding BBQ!"). #### **Option 2: The Compromise (If You Want to Stay Involved)** If you **don’t want to fully cut yourself off**, suggest: - **"I can’t be a groomsman, but I’d love to be your ‘honorary uncle’ or just come as a guest!"** (This keeps you involved without the pressure.) - **"Can I bring a plus-one?"** (If you have a friend who’d be great support.) - **"I can’t be there on the 25th, but I’ll be there for the rehearsal dinner!"** #### **Option 3: The "I Need Time" Staller (If You’re Unsure)** *"Wow, that’s so cool! I need to think about it—I’ve got a lot on my plate right now, but I’ll get back to you by [date]."* (Then decide based on your comfort level.) --- ### **What If He Gets Upset?** - **He might say:** *"But you’re my best friend!"* - **Reply:** *"I am, and I want you to know I’ll always be here for you—just not in that way right now."* - **He might say:** *"Your ex is just a friend, it’s not a big deal."* - **Reply:** *"It’s not about her—it’s about what’s best for me right now. I don’t want to let anything ruin this day for you, but I also can’t force myself to be somewhere I’ll be uncomfortable."* - **He might try to guilt-trip you.** - **Stay firm:** *"I’m not saying no to you—I’m saying no to this specific role. I hope you can respect that."* --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (You’re Not the Asshole)** **You’re not obligated to put yourself in a position that risks your mental health.** A true friend will: ✅ **Respect your boundaries** (even if it’s hard for him). ✅ **Find other ways to include you** (e.g., "Can you give the toast?" or "I’ll save you a dance!"). ✅ **Understand that your healing isn’t a burden.** **If he can’t handle this, that’s a bigger problem than your decline.** A real friend will celebrate you for setting limits—not punish you for them. --- ### **Aftermath Tips** - **If you decline:** Plan a **separate celebration** with him (e.g., a post-wedding dinner just the two of you). - **If you accept:** **Set ground rules** (e.g., "I’ll only stay for X hours" or "I’m not engaging with [ex] at all"). - **If you’re unsure:** Ask yourself: - *Will I regret not going?* - *Will I regret going?* - *Is there a middle ground?* --- ### **TL;DR** You’re **not the asshole** for prioritizing your well-being. His reaction will tell you **how much he truly values your friendship**—not your willingness to endure discomfort. **Your peace is worth more than any wedding role.** Would you like help drafting a message to him?
